Vascular Disorders of the CNS

Neuro · Week 2
LO 1–4 Atherosclerotic ~10% of ischemic strokes Anterior circulation

🩸 Carotid Stenosis

▶
▶ Understanding Carotid Artery Stenosis
Video — "Understanding Carotid Artery Stenosis" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 68-year-old man is brought in after his daughter noticed he seemed to lose vision in his right eye for about ten minutes the day before, describing it as "a curtain coming down," with complete return to normal by the time he was evaluated. He has a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a 40-pack-year smoking history. On auscultation of the neck, a bruit is heard over the right carotid area. Which of the following is the most likely underlying mechanism?

1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Atherosclerotic, degenerative disease of the common and internal carotid arteries — narrowing almost always occurs within 2 cm of the carotid bifurcation.

  • Prevalence ~1.5% in adults age 30–79
  • Accounts for an estimated 10% of ischemic strokes; incidence of new carotid-related stroke ~1.6 per 1,000
  • Of patients with a carotid bruit, 35% have ≥50% stenosis
  • Risk factors: advanced age, male sex, White race, tobacco use, hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia
Pathophysiology

The clinical danger is an artery-to-artery embolic mechanism — the plaque itself is usually the embolic source, not necessarily a flow-limiting occlusion.

Atherosclerotic plaque
→
Progressive luminal narrowing
→
Plaque fissure / thrombus
→
Distal embolization
→
MCA–ACA watershed infarct

Prognosis if untreated tracks directly with % stenosis: stroke risk is >1%/yr at 80% stenosis, rising to 4.8%/yr at 90%. Even asymptomatic stenosis >50% carries a 0.5–1%/yr stroke risk.

2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Most patients are asymptomatic, picked up incidentally via a bruit. Symptomatic disease reflects anterior-circulation ischemia:

  • Contralateral weakness / paralysis
  • Contralateral numbness, sensory loss, or paresthesia
  • Dysarthria or dysphasia
  • Ipsilateral monocular vision loss (amaurosis fugax) — ophthalmic artery territory
  • Contralateral visual field deficit

Exam findings: carotid bruit (turbulent flow), Hollenhorst plaque on fundoscopy (cholesterol embolus lodged at a retinal arteriole bifurcation).

Transient Ischemic Attack

  • Focal deficit resolving in <24h (classic definition)
  • Proposed tissue-based definition: <1h, no infarct on imaging

Ischemic Stroke

  • Focal or generalized deficit persisting >24h
  • Same anterior-circulation symptom pattern as TIA, just sustained / infarct present
Red Flags / Risk Stratification

Combined motor + sensory + speech deficit → ~5% stroke risk at 48 hours. Sensory deficit alone → ~0% stroke risk at 48 hours.

Carotid stenosis does not typically cause vertigo, lightheadedness, or syncope — those point toward posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulation instead.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Screen by auscultating for a carotid bruit; anyone with a bruit should get imagingCarotid duplex ultrasound — first-line; shows focally increased peak systolic velocity, increased intima-media thickness, or absent flow if occluded
Hollenhorst plaque on fundoscopic examCTA or MRA — confirmatory; evaluates head + neck vessels simultaneously in stroke/TIA workup; MRA tends to overestimate stenosis, CTA preferred if MRI contraindicated
—Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) — gold standard, but invasive with its own stroke/mortality risk; reserved for inconclusive noninvasive imaging or preprocedural planning
Duplex ultrasound — right proximal ICA, elevated peak systolic velocity (~146 cm/s) on spectral Doppler, consistent with hemodynamically significant stenosis
MR angiography, neck vessels — high-grade stenosis at the origin of the right internal carotid artery
CT angiography, neck — luminal narrowing of the carotid artery at the bifurcation
4 · Treatment
Treatment

ASCVD-directed medical therapy is lifelong for every patient and continues even after revascularization.

Medical

  • High-intensity statin, indefinitely
  • Single-agent antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel); short DAPT course after stenting
  • Risk factor control: smoking cessation, BP and glucose management

Surgical — CEA

  • Carotid endarterectomy: first-line if good surgical candidate
  • Lower periprocedural stroke risk than stenting, especially age >70
  • Higher periprocedural MI risk; risk of cranial nerve palsy

Endovascular — CAS

  • Carotid artery stenting: preferred when surgical access/risk is poor (e.g. irradiated neck)
  • Higher periprocedural stroke risk than CEA

Revascularization is indicated for symptomatic severe (70–99%) stenosis if life expectancy ≥2 years and operator risk is acceptable (<6%), ideally within 14 days of symptom onset. For asymptomatic severe stenosis, consider it only if procedural risk is low (<3%).

Management algorithm — duplex confirms stenosis, then revascularization decision hinges on degree of stenosis and symptomatic status
Carotid angiography before (a) and after (b) stent placement — occlusion at the carotid bulb recanalized after stenting
Pearl

Sensory-only TIA symptoms carry ~0% 48-hour stroke risk, but adding motor or speech involvement jumps that to ~5% — it's the combination, not any single symptom, that should trigger urgent workup.

🧠 Practice Questions — Carotid Stenosis
LO 1–6 ~80–85% of strokes Time is brain Large + small vessel

🧠 Ischemic Stroke

▶
▶ Ischemic Stroke — causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology
Video — "Ischemic Stroke - causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, pathology" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation who is not taking anticoagulation is brought to the emergency department after acutely developing right facial droop, right arm weakness, and difficulty speaking approximately 90 minutes ago while watching television. Blood pressure is 178/94 mmHg and fingerstick glucose is 110 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step?

1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Ischemic infarction is the most common cause of stroke — accounts for 80–85% of all strokes (~20% of these in the vertebrobasilar system). The most frequent inpatient neurologic problem in a general hospital.

  • ~800,000 first-time strokes/year in the US; ~135,000 annual deaths; projected to approach 1 million/year by 2050
  • Nonmodifiable: age ≥65 (strongest nonmodifiable factor), male sex, Black/Native American/Alaska Native/Hispanic ethnicity, family history, sickle cell disease, prior TIA, migraine with aura, low birth weight
  • Modifiable: hypertension (strongest modifiable factor), hyperlipidemia, diabetes, atherosclerosis, atrial fibrillation, carotid stenosis, obesity, hypercoagulable states, heavy alcohol use, smoking, cocaine use, OCP/HRT use, sedentary lifestyle, poor diet
Pathophysiology — Mechanism

Determining the mechanism is the first, critical step toward preventing recurrence:

Thrombotic (~40%)

  • Large-vessel atherosclerosis (~20%) — plaque rupture at branch points (e.g. ICA bifurcation)
  • Small-vessel lipohyalinosis (~20%) — lacunar infarcts
  • Most common cause overall; often preceded by a heralding TIA; up to 60% occur during sleep

Embolic (~20–30%)

  • Cardiac source (Afib, mural thrombus, valve disease) — 25–30% of infarctions
  • Artery-to-artery (carotid atheroembolus)
  • Paradoxical embolism via PFO/ASD; "spectacular shrinking deficit" as the clot migrates distally

Global Ischemia

  • Systemic hypoperfusion (shock, cardiac surgery) → watershed infarct
  • Severe/chronic hypoxia, recurrent hypoglycemia
Mechanism overview — lacunar & atherothrombotic (thrombotic), embolus lodging distal to the ICA/MCA junction (embolic), and bilateral watershed injury (global ischemia)

CBF thresholds: normal ~50 cc/100g/min → electrophysiologic silence ≤20 → irreversible injury ≤10.

30 sec: metabolism altered
→
1 min: neuronal function ceases
→
5 min: infarction begins
→
6–12h: coagulative necrosis, red neurons
→
3–4 days: liquefaction

Infarcted tissue organizes into a core necrotic zone, a salvageable penumbra, and a surrounding region of edema at risk for herniation.

Lacunar Infarct

  • Chronic HTN → lipohyalinosis of penetrating arteries (e.g. lenticulostriate)
  • No cortical signs (no aphasia, hemianopsia, agnosia, apraxia)
  • Pure motor (most common — posterior limb internal capsule), pure sensory (rare), sensorimotor, dysarthria-clumsy hand, ataxic hemiparesis

Watershed (Border-Zone) Infarct

  • Systemic hypoperfusion between two vascular territories
  • ACA–MCA border → "man-in-the-barrel" (proximal weakness, face/hand/foot spared)
  • MCA–PCA border → bilateral cortical blindness
Watershed zones — cortical border zones (ACA–MCA, MCA–PCA) and internal border zones between superficial and deep MCA branches
MRI (FLAIR A/B, DWI a/b) — cortical border-zone infarct at the MCA–PCA boundary (a) and an internal (deep MCA) watershed infarct (b)
Histologic TimelineFindings
12–24 hoursRed neurons (eosinophilic cytoplasm, pyknotic nucleus)
1–3 daysNeutrophils; liquefactive necrosis
3–5 daysMacrophages (microglia)
5–15 daysReactive gliosis, vascular proliferation
>15 daysGlial scarring, cyst formation
Mnemonic

Most vulnerable regions to hypoxia — hippocampus, neocortex, Purkinje cells, watershed areas: "Vulnerable hippos Need PURe water."

2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Sudden focal neurologic deficits — weakness/paralysis, paresthesia, aphasia, dysarthria — often with nonspecific findings (altered consciousness, nausea/vomiting, headache, seizure).

Embolic

  • "Bolt out of the blue" — maximal deficit at onset
  • Rapidly evolves to a completed stroke
  • Often follows a cardiac event

Thrombotic

  • >50% preceded by a heralding TIA
  • Can stutter/progress over hours to days
  • Up to 60% occur during sleep

Etiology clues

  • Aortic dissection: chest pain, hypotension, dyspnea
  • Endocarditis: fever, murmur
  • ICH/SAH mimic: sudden severe headache
Stroke Mimics / Red Flags

Check glucose immediately — severe hypo/hyperglycemia is a common stroke mimic. A first-time seizure with a postictal (Todd's) paralysis can also mimic stroke — always rule out an acute structural cause.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Establish time last known well; NIHSS severity assessment; modified Rankin Scale for baseline/outcome disabilityPOC glucose first — rule out a metabolic mimic
Focal exam: lateralizing signs, GCS, pupils, herniation screenNoncontrast CT head — first-line, fast; rules out hemorrhage/mimics before any reperfusion therapy
Cardiac auscultation for murmur; assess for arrhythmiaMRI brain (DWI) — most sensitive for early infarct; used for wake-up/unclear-onset strokes via DWI–FLAIR mismatch
—CTA head/neck (most common), MRA, carotid duplex, TCD, or DSA (invasive gold standard) — vessel/occlusion mapping
—Labs: glucose, troponin, coagulation panel, BMP, CBC; ECG + ≥24h cardiac monitoring for all patients (occult Afib); echocardiography if embolic source suspected
Noncontrast CT head — hyperdense right MCA sign, a marker of MCA thrombus visible before parenchymal changes appear
CT Timeline Pearl

<6h: hypodense parenchyma, loss of gray-white differentiation, sulcal effacement → 12–24h: better demarcated → 3–5 days: maximum edema → 2–3 weeks: transient isodense "fogging" → chronic: hypodense, well-demarcated, negative mass effect.

4 · Treatment
Reperfusion Therapy — Time Is Brain

IV Thrombolysis (alteplase / tenecteplase)

  • <3h: any eligible patient ≥18 with a disabling deficit
  • 3–4.5h: select patients (neurology consult)
  • Unclear onset / wake-up stroke: MRI DWI–FLAIR mismatch determines eligibility
  • Absolute contraindications: recent ICH/stroke/surgery, active bleeding, INR>1.7, platelets<100k, uncontrolled BP >185/110

Mechanical Thrombectomy

  • Large-vessel occlusion (e.g. ICA, MCA-M1)
  • Window extends to 24h from last known normal in selected patients with favorable imaging
Management algorithm — noncontrast imaging first, then thrombolysis/thrombectomy eligibility based on time window and contraindications
Supportive Care & Underlying Cause
  • BP: permissive hypertension if not undergoing reperfusion (tolerate up to 220/120 first 48–72h); if undergoing reperfusion, keep <185/110 pre- and <180/105 for 24h post-treatment (labetalol, clevidipine, nicardipine)
  • Antiplatelet: aspirin or clopidogrel started 24–48h after onset (wait ≥24h post-thrombolysis)
  • Glucose: treat if <60 or maintain 140–180 mg/dL; temperature: treat fever >38°C
  • Treat underlying cause: carotid endarterectomy/stenting within 2–7 days for relevant symptomatic carotid stenosis; anticoagulation for Afib; antithrombotics 3–6 months for arterial dissection
  • Dysphagia screen before oral intake, VTE prophylaxis, early rehab (PT/OT/speech), depression screening
5 · Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring & Complications
  • High risk of early recurrence in the acute period
  • Cytotoxic edema → herniation (subfalcine, transtentorial, uncal, transcalvarial) — peaks 3–5 days; malignant MCA or large PICA/cerebellar infarcts may need surgical decompression before edema peaks
  • Hemorrhagic transformation — embolic strokes convert to hemorrhage more often than thrombotic strokes
  • Post-thrombolysis: frequent BP/neuro checks; follow-up CT/MRI at 24h before starting anticoagulant/antiplatelet therapy
  • Thrombolysis complications: angioedema (airway risk), intracranial or extracranial hemorrhage
6 · Prevention & Health Promotion
Secondary Prevention
  • Long-term antiplatelet therapy for noncardioembolic stroke; anticoagulation for cardioembolic sources (e.g. Afib)
  • Carotid endarterectomy/stenting only when specific criteria for relevant stenosis are met
  • Hypertension control — the single most important modifiable risk factor for preventing recurrence
  • Statin therapy, glycemic control, smoking cessation, weight loss, OSA screening/CPAP, reducing alcohol use, diet and exercise counseling
Pearl

Embolic strokes are more prone to hemorrhagic transformation than thrombotic strokes — a useful distinction when deciding how soon to (re)start anticoagulation after a cardioembolic event.

🧠 Practice Questions — Ischemic Stroke
LO 1–3 No infarct on imaging ~1/3 → future stroke

⏱️ Transient Ischemic Attack

▶
▶ 2-Minute Neuroscience: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)
Video — "2-Minute Neuroscience: Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA)" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 68-year-old woman reports that during breakfast she suddenly could not find the right words to describe her coffee and felt her right hand go weak. Both symptoms resolved completely over about 20 minutes, and she now feels entirely normal. She has hypertension and a history of paroxysmal palpitations. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Episodes of stroke symptoms lasting less than 24 hours (most resolve in ~12 minutes) that do not terminate in stroke — imaging shows no infarct.

  • ~240,000 TIAs occur annually in the US (revised upward from an earlier conservative estimate of 50,000/year once out-of-hospital events and broader demographics were captured)
  • For roughly one third of patients, a TIA is not an isolated event — it signals an impending stroke
  • Stroke risk after TIA: 10–15% within the first 3 months; ~33% lifetime risk
  • Risk stratified with the ABCD2 score; risk factors for stroke after TIA: age >60, hypertension, weakness or speech disturbance during the TIA, duration >60 minutes, diabetes mellitus
Pathophysiology

Mechanistically identical to ischemic stroke at the outset — embolism or thrombus compromises a vessel — except the vessel reopens spontaneously before infarction occurs. Risk factors mirror those for ischemic stroke (see that panel).

Embolic

  • Single, discrete episode
  • Lasts hours

Lacunar / Small Vessel

  • Symptoms build gradually
  • Lasts hours to days

Large Vessel / Low-Flow

  • Recurrent episodes
  • Lasts minutes
TIA overview — cardioembolic (Afib) and atherosclerotic-thrombus etiologies; symptom duration varies by underlying mechanism as outlined above
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Transient focal neurologic signs or symptoms — lasting anywhere from seconds to minutes, but always <24 hours by the classic definition.

  • Most TIAs last <15 minutes; 90% resolve within an hour
  • Symptom pattern mirrors stroke for the affected territory, including possible amaurosis fugax — the difference is complete resolution with no residual deficit
Key Distinction

TIA is now a tissue-based, not time-based, diagnosis: a transient deficit with a positive infarct on imaging is classified as a stroke regardless of how quickly symptoms resolved.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Rule out metabolic or drug-induced mimicsFingerstick glucose, CBC, electrolytes, coagulation studies, ECG with rhythm strip, ESR, cardiac enzymes, lipid profile
Consider hypercoagulable/inflammatory causes in select patientsAdditional labs as indicated: hypercoagulable workup, syphilis serology, antiphospholipid antibodies, toxicology screen, hemoglobin/serum protein electrophoresis, CSF exam
—Brain imaging within 24h of onset: MRI with DWI (preferred); noncontrast CT if MRI unavailable; carotid duplex, CTA, or MRA to evaluate vasculature
Initial management pathway — if symptoms have resolved, MRI within 24h looking for signs of reversible ischemia is what confirms TIA (vs. an infarct, which reclassifies the event as stroke)
Pearl

Don't let symptom resolution lower your guard — a TIA carries a 10–15% stroke risk in just the first three months, which is exactly why urgent workup (not reassurance) is the standard of care.

🧠 Practice Questions — Transient Ischemic Attack
LO 1–6 10–15% of strokes ~40% mortality HTN-driven

🩸 Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage

▶
▶ USMLE ACE Video 209: Comprehensive Guide to Hemorrhagic Brain Stroke
Video — "USMLE ACE Video 209: Comprehensive Guide to Hemorrhagic Brain Stroke" (YouTube) — link is timestamped to start at 14:10
🎯 How boards would word it

A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension is brought to the emergency department after his wife found him confused and unable to move his right side. He reports a sudden, severe headache that began about 45 minutes ago, followed by nausea and vomiting. On exam, his eyes are deviated toward the left. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Bleeding within the brain parenchyma (± extension into the ventricular system). Distinct from the broader term intracranial hemorrhage, which also includes epidural, subdural, and subarachnoid bleeding.

  • Incidence ~12–15 per 100,000/year (up to 350 per 100,000 hypertensive elderly individuals); strongly age-dependent
  • Accounts for 10–15% of all strokes
  • Incidence is 2× higher in individuals of Asian or African descent; overall incidence has declined since the 1950s (better BP control)
  • Hypertensive hemorrhage: 50–60% of all ICH — the leading cause overall
  • Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA): most common cause in patients >60 years old
  • Sympathomimetic drugs (e.g. cocaine): leading cause in young patients
  • Other causes: AVMs, vasculitis, neoplasms, hemorrhagic transformation of an ischemic stroke, head trauma
Pathophysiology

Hypertensive (deep) hemorrhage

Chronic HTN
→
Lipohyalinosis / Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms
→
Lenticulostriate vessel rupture

Descending frequency: putamen > thalamus > cerebellum > pons

Amyloid angiopathy (lobar)

β-amyloid deposition in vessel walls
→
Microaneurysm formation
→
Rupture — recurrent lobar hemorrhage

Cortical/lobar distribution — the key feature that distinguishes it from hypertensive deep hemorrhage.

Bleeding may stay confined to parenchyma or rupture into the ventricles (intraventricular hemorrhage, contaminating the CSF) — parenchymal bleeding almost never breaches the outer cortical surface, so blood found in the CSF is usually tracking in via the ventricles. IVH is an ominous prognostic sign.

Prognosis if untreated: overall mortality ~40% (in-hospital death rate ~60%); of survivors, only 1 in 5 return to independent living.

2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Sudden focal neurologic deficit, often progressively worsening, commonly with headache and nausea — more prominent than in ischemic stroke. Can rapidly progress (in <1 day) to loss of consciousness from rising ICP; midline shift may be visible on imaging.

Putaminal Hemorrhage

  • Contralateral hemiparesis/hemiplegia
  • Contralateral hemisensory loss (less severe)
  • Eyes deviate toward the side of the hematoma

Thalamic Hemorrhage

  • Contralateral hemiparesis + hemisensory loss
  • Decreased consciousness
  • "Wrong-way eyes"
Late Course / Red Flags

Late signs reflect rising ICP: nausea/vomiting, confusion, and progressive loss of consciousness — a rapidly evolving exam is a neurosurgical emergency, not a "watch and wait" situation.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
TimingLabsImaging
First hourCoagulation panel + INR, CBC (rule out thrombocytopenia), POC glucoseCT head without contrast (gold standard); MRI as an alternative
Hours to daysElectrolytes, BUN/Cr, troponin, tox screen, pregnancy test, UA/cultureCT angiography (or MRA); CT/MRI venogram if venous thrombosis suspected; cerebral angiography if a structural lesion is suspected
Noncontrast CT — large hyperdense hematoma in the posterior left hemisphere with surrounding hypodense edema, effacement of the occipital horn, and midline shift
Noncontrast CT — lobar hemorrhage from a ruptured left MCA aneurysm, with extensive subarachnoid blood in the basal cisterns and fissures, plus obstructive ventricular dilatation
Density Timeline Pearl

CT: hyperacute (<24h) and acute (1–3d) → hyperdense → early subacute (>3d–1wk) → hyperdense fading to isodense → late subacute (weeks–months) → isodense/hypodense → chronic (>months) → hypodense. MRI (T2) runs roughly the opposite: hyperintense early, hypointense mid-course, hyperintense again late.

4 · Treatment
Treatment
  • Manage underlying/associated conditions to limit hematoma expansion: control hypertension, reverse coagulopathy
  • Osmotherapy (mannitol) and hyperventilation for elevated ICP when indicated
  • Early surgical decompression for large cerebellar hematomas — the confined posterior fossa leaves little room before brainstem compression occurs
  • External ventricular drainage (EVD) for developing hydrocephalus
  • Neurosurgical consultation for all significant hemorrhages
  • Traumatic ICH is managed similarly to spontaneous ICH
5 · Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring & Complications
  • Edema and hemispheric herniation from elevated ICP
  • Careful management of anticoagulation — both reversal acutely and timing of restart
  • Progressive loss of consciousness as a marker of clinical deterioration
  • Overall ~40% mortality; ~60% in-hospital death rate; only 1 in 5 survivors regain independent living
6 · Prevention & Health Promotion
Prevention

Early, aggressive management of hypertension is the primary preventive strategy — it is both the leading cause of ICH and the single most modifiable risk factor.

Pearl

Eyes deviate toward a destructive supratentorial lesion like a hemorrhage — opposite to an active seizure focus, which drives gaze away from the irritated hemisphere.

🧠 Practice Questions — Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage
LO 1–6 ~3% of strokes ~40% mortality 85% aneurysmal

💥 Subarachnoid Hemorrhage

▶
▶ 2-Minute Neuroscience: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
Video — "2-Minute Neuroscience: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 52-year-old woman develops the sudden onset of the "worst headache of her life" while lifting weights at the gym, followed by neck stiffness and one episode of vomiting. She is awake but uncomfortable, with photophobia and a positive Kernig sign. Noncontrast CT of the head, obtained 10 hours after symptom onset, is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Bleeding into the subarachnoid space surrounding the brain — a form of stroke. The nearly exclusive nontraumatic cause is a ruptured saccular (berry) aneurysm; overall, traumatic SAH (head trauma) is more common than spontaneous SAH.

  • Annual incidence of nontraumatic aneurysmal SAH: 6–25 per 100,000; >27,000 Americans/year suffer a ruptured intracranial aneurysm
  • Incidence rises with age and is likely underestimated (deaths often attributed to other causes without autopsy confirmation)
  • Incidence is 2× higher in individuals of African, Asian, or Hispanic descent vs. Caucasian
  • Accounts for only ~3% of all strokes — 4th most common stroke type, behind embolism, thrombosis, and intracerebral hemorrhage

Etiology breakdown: aneurysmal rupture (85%) > perimesencephalic bleeding in the ambient cistern (10%) > AVMs / other rare causes (5%, sometimes triggered by an acute BP rise or physical exertion).

  • Risk factors: smoking, hypertension, family history of SAH; aneurysm formation is largely idiopathic but linked to genetics, age, and toxins (alcohol, smoking)
  • Associated comorbidities: polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type IV, neurofibromatosis type 1
Pathophysiology

Most aneurysms form at arterial bifurcation/trifurcation points, likely from idiopathic wall weakness combined with hemodynamic stress at the junction. Because bleeding enters the subarachnoid space directly, blood contaminates the CSF — xanthochromic CSF is pathognomonic for SAH (unlike parenchymal ICH, which usually requires ventricular rupture to reach the CSF).

Common aneurysm sites — ACA/anterior communicating artery (~40%) > internal carotid artery (~30%) > MCA (~20%) > basilar/vertebral arteries (~10%); the anterior circle of Willis dominates overall
Circle of Willis anatomy — the shared origin point for the great majority of saccular (berry) aneurysms

Prognosis if untreated: 10–14% die before ever reaching the hospital; overall mortality is ~40%, with most deaths occurring within the first 24 hours.

2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Ranges from completely normal to deeply comatose at presentation.

  • Thunderclap headache — sudden, severe, "worst of my life" — though only reported in ~20% of patients by some estimates; don't anchor on headache severity alone
  • Meningeal signs (Kernig, Brudzinski) present in about one third of patients
  • Nonspecific: impaired consciousness, focal deficits from mass effect, seizures
  • Sentinel bleed: a sudden but mild headache — especially with transient cranial nerve dysfunction — can be a warning sign of impending major rupture
  • Cushing response: rising ICP triggers hypertension, as if the cranial vault were a closed pressurized container
3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamLabs / Imaging
Meningeal signs, sentinel-bleed history, Cushing responseNoncontrast CT head — best initial test; sensitivity near 100% within 6h of onset; shows hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, and sulci
—Lumbar puncture if CT is negative but suspicion remains — pink/red or xanthochromic CSF, elevated RBC count
—CTA as an alternative second-line test; once SAH is confirmed, angiography is always needed — DSA is the gold standard for localizing the aneurysm and planning treatment
Noncontrast CT — multiple areas of high attenuation in the basal cisterns, Sylvian fissures, and sulci, characteristic of extensive SAH
Noncontrast CT — extensive SAH in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures, with a focal rounded hemorrhage adjacent to the left cerebral peduncle suggesting a posterior communicating or posterior cerebral artery aneurysm; mild ventricular dilatation also visible
Key Pitfall

A CT negative for SAH does not rule it out if clinical suspicion remains high — especially beyond the 6-hour high-sensitivity window. Proceed to LP or CTA rather than reassuring the patient.

4 · Treatment
Aneurysm Repair

Endovascular Coiling

  • Minimally invasive — catheter-delivered metal coils induce thrombotic occlusion
  • Higher risk of incomplete obliteration / recurrent bleeding
  • Favored for: poor surgical candidates, posterior circulation aneurysms, vasospasm, large ICH with elevated ICP

Microsurgical Clipping

  • More invasive — craniotomy with titanium clip across the aneurysm neck
  • Higher complete occlusion rate; lower rebleeding risk
  • Favored for: MCA aneurysms, difficult endovascular access, failed endovascular attempt

Further management: oral nimodipine to reduce vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischemia risk; drainage/shunt placement for hydrocephalus when indicated; clot removal only when indicated; historically, "triple-H" therapy (hypertension, hypervolemia, hemodilution) has also been used, alongside general neuroprotective measures and BP control.

5 · Monitoring & Complications
Monitoring & Complications

Rebleeding

  • Occurs in 4–14% of patients, mostly within the first 24 hours
  • Drives the urgency of early aneurysm repair

Vasospasm

  • Typically occurs 3–10 days after SAH
  • Blood breakdown products release vasoactive substances → diffuse cerebral vasospasm → can progress to ischemic stroke
  • Impaired CSF reabsorption at the arachnoid villi also drives communicating hydrocephalus → ↑ICP → ↓cerebral perfusion pressure → ischemia
  • Hydrocephalus: acute obstructive or chronic communicating
  • Elevated ICP: hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing (Cushing triad)
  • Seizures
  • SIADH → hyponatremia from vasopressin (ADH) oversecretion
6 · Prevention & Health Promotion
Prevention
  • Prevention/control of hypertension
  • Smoking cessation
  • Moderation of alcohol use
Pearl

Time-shift your differential for delayed decline after SAH: a decline in the first 24 hours is rebleeding until proven otherwise, while a decline at day 3–10 is vasospasm until proven otherwise.

🧠 Practice Questions — Subarachnoid Hemorrhage
LO 1–3 1/10 as common as aneurysms ~3% bleed risk/yr

🌀 Vascular Malformations

▶
▶ Arteriovenous Malformations (AVMs) | Surgical Treatment Options at UCSF
Video — "Arteriovenous Malformations (AVMs) | Surgical Treatment Options at UCSF" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 22-year-old man presents with a new-onset focal seizure and a several-month history of unilateral, migraine-like headaches. On examination, a bruit is auscultated over the skull. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

1 · Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

A tangled mass of dilated vessels embedded in the brain — a source of hemorrhagic stroke and, separately, a cause of seizure disorder. Vascular malformations divide into four types:

Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM)

  • Most common type
  • High-flow — arteries shunt directly into veins

Cavernous Malformation

  • Low-flow cluster of dilated, thin-walled vessels
  • No normal brain tissue interposed — prone to microhemorrhage

Capillary Telangiectasia

  • Cluster of dilated capillaries with normal brain tissue in between
  • Usually incidental, low risk

Venous Angioma (DVA)

  • Anomalous but functional draining veins in a "caput medusae" pattern
  • Generally benign, low bleed risk
  • AVMs are ~1/10 as common as saccular aneurysms; 1:1 male-to-female ratio
  • Most AVMs are congenital; can occur in the cerebrum, cerebellum, brainstem, or spinal cord — the largest are typically cerebral
  • Annual bleed risk ~3%/year
Pathophysiology

An AVM reflects a persistent embryonic vascular pattern — arteries connect directly to veins, bypassing the normal capillary network. A KRAS oncogene mutation has been implicated in some cases, though AVMs are not considered neoplasms.

Normal vs. AVM — in a normal network, arteries feed capillaries that slowly deliver oxygen before draining into veins; in an AVM, blood shunts quickly from artery straight to vein, bypassing that capillary bed
AVM anatomy — a tangled nidus fed by dilated arteries and drained by dilated, high-flow veins

Consequences of this abnormal architecture:

  • "Steal" phenomenon — shunted flow diverts blood away from adjacent normal brain, which can itself produce an ischemic deficit
  • Mass effect from compression of surrounding structures

Cavernous Malformation

Cavernoma — a low-flow cluster of dilated, thin-walled vessels with feeding arteries and a draining vein

Venous Angioma (DVA)

Developmental venous anomaly — anomalous but functional draining veins converging in a radial pattern
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Can remain clinically silent for life. When symptomatic, onset is most common between ages 10–30. Presentation is usually acute, though insidious symptoms can occur from compression of surrounding structures.

  • Headache — typically migraine-type
  • Focal seizures (~30% of cases)
  • Intracerebral hemorrhage of varying size (~90% survival if it bleeds)
  • Large AVMs may present with an audible bruit — a high-flow finding you won't see with the other three subtypes
3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamImaging
Cranial auscultation for a bruit; seizure or headache historyMRI — flow voids from the tangled high-flow nidus; MRA for vascular detail
—CT with contrast; catheter (X-ray) angiography for definitive vascular mapping before any intervention
Axial T2 MRI — numerous serpiginous flow voids in the right hemisphere, characteristic of a large AVM nidus (case courtesy of Frank Gaillard, Radiopaedia.org, case rID 4000)
Pearl

AVMs can cause a deficit two different ways — a hemorrhage from vessel rupture, or an ischemic "steal" deficit in adjacent tissue even without any bleeding at all.

🦴 Spinal Cord Infarction

▶
▶ USMLE/UWorld - Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome, Anterior Spinal Cord Syndrome
Video — "USMLE/UWorld - Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome, Anterior Spinal Cord Syndrome" (YouTube)
🎯 How boards would word it

A 68-year-old man undergoes emergency repair of a ruptured thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Twelve hours postoperatively, he is noted to have flaccid weakness of both legs with absent pain and temperature sensation below the umbilicus, but preserved vibration and proprioception. Which of the following vessels is most likely responsible for this presentation?

1 · Natural History
Anatomy & Epidemiology

The spinal cord is supplied by three small arteries — a single midline anterior spinal artery (ASA) and paired posterior spinal arteries near the posterolateral sulcus. The ASA is the largest of the three and the only one that infarcts with any real frequency.

  • The ASA is fed by 5–6 medullary arteries (branches of the vertebral, intercostal, or lumbar arteries) — medullary arteries are larger than the segmental radicular arteries, which instead enter every intervertebral foramen mainly to perfuse the nerve roots
  • The dorsolateral cord is separately supplied by the corona radiata (a pial arterial plexus)
  • Estimated to account for ~1.2% of stroke admissions
Spinal cord blood supply (cross-section) — the anterior spinal artery (via the sulcal artery) perfuses the anterior two-thirds, including the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts; the posterior spinal arteries and circumferential/pial plexus supply the dorsal columns and dorsolateral cord
Etiology & Pathophysiology

Causes of ASA infarction are varied: aortic atheroma, surgical aortic repair, collagen vascular disease, syphilis, dissecting aortic aneurysm, embolic infarction, radiographic contrast injection, mass effect from a nearby tumor, and systemic arterial hypotension.

  • Several medullary arteries supply the cervical and upper thoracic cord
  • The great medullary artery of Adamkiewicz supplies the lumbosacral cord — typically arising around T9–T12 from a posterior intercostal branch off the aorta
  • A watershed zone exists around T8–T10, where the ASA is too small on its own to perfuse across the gap
  • Infarcts of the artery of Adamkiewicz therefore typically take out the cord from roughly T8–T10 downward — which is exactly why aortic surgery in this region is a recognized risk
Artery of Adamkiewicz — arising near the T9 vertebral level from a posterior intercostal artery off the aorta, joining the anterior spinal artery to supply the lumbosacral cord
2 · Clinical Presentation
Presentation
  • Acute onset
  • Back pain, often radiating into the legs
  • Weakness below the level of the lesion — initially flaccid paralysis (spinal shock), which can evolve into spasticity over time
  • Autonomic dysfunction below the lesion — bowel/bladder incontinence can occur
  • Analgesia (loss of pain/temperature sensation) below the lesion
  • Sparing of vibratory and proprioceptive sense — the hallmark dissociated sensory pattern
Localizing Pearl

The dissociated sensory loss is the whole story here: pain/temperature and motor function run through the anterior two-thirds of the cord (ASA territory), while vibration/proprioception travel in the dorsal columns (posterior spinal artery territory) — hence the sparing.

3 · Diagnostic Workup
History / Physical ExamImaging / Labs
Acute back pain with a dissociated sensory pattern below a spinal level; recent aortic surgery or hypotensive episodeMRI (T1 & T2) — confirms the infarct and rules out a compressive neoplasm
—Lumbar puncture — excludes hemorrhage or an inflammatory/infectious myelopathy (e.g. transverse myelitis, epidural abscess) that can mimic this presentation
Pearl

Anterior spinal artery syndrome spares vibration and proprioception because those posterior column pathways are supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries, not the single anterior spinal artery — a clean way to localize the lesion to the cord's anterior two-thirds.
